newsitem.title: THAILAND: Laos faces challenges in development, ADB says.
newsitem.headline: Laos faces challenges in development, ADB says.

text.p: Laos has begun the process of liberalisation but still must implement a programme to develop its economy, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) said on Thursday.
"The Lao People's Democratic Republic has established the basic elements of a market-oriented system," said the ADB annual report.

"The country now faces the challenge of putting into place an effective development programme to increase domestic resource mobilisation, further monetise the economy and undertake basic infrastructure development."

Laos' economy grew by 6.9 percent in 1996 compared with the 1991-1995 average growth of 6.1 percent, the ADB report said. Agriculture, which accounts for more than half of the gross domestic product (GDP) was again affected by floods but grew by 3.0 percent for the year.
The ADB predicted Laos' GDP would grow by 8.0-8.5 percent a year between 1996-2000, but 1997 growth was expected to be below that range at 7.2 percent.
Measures to control inflation had been largely successful, the ADB report said, with the consumer price index rising about 14 percent for the year compared to a 19.4 percent rise in 1995.
Trade had expanded rapidly in recent years, ADB said, to 53.7 percent of GDP in 1996 from 37.7 percent in 1988.
"Lao PDR faces the problems typical of many other landlocked countries, including a high dependence on its trading neighbours," the report said.
"In 1996, more than 69 percent of exports were destined for Thailand or Vietnam, which together also accounted for over 75 percent of imports."
The ADB said Laos' current account deficit was expected to worsen in the next two years as export volumes were likely to drop further in 1997 but improve in 1998.
The weakness in the country's foreign exchange system may continue to pose some threat to economic stability, since the economy is vulnerable to foreign exchange outflows.

"Foreign exchange is in extremely short supply and will remain so until the government generates substantial foreign exchange revenues from its hydroelectric projects, and until new export industries are developed in products for which the economy has a potential comparative advantage," the report said.
